achievement_drive.rationale: Won three FIFA World Cups (1958, 1962, 1970) across three separate career phases, a documented competitive outcome suggesting sustained ambition, though this is scored from results rather than a specific documented behavioral account of his training or preparation approach.

competitiveness.rationale: Sustained elite performance across three World Cup cycles evidences real competitive drive, though — as with achievement_drive — this is inferred substantially from results rather than specific documented personal behavior.

discipline.rationale: A multi-decade elite athletic career implies sustained training discipline, but readily available sourcing documents match outcomes and statistics far more thoroughly than his personal working habits or routine.

holdReason: Scored only 3 attributes at low confidence — the same evidence-type gap identified for Jesse Owens in the first batch, and genuinely more severe here: readily available English-language sourcing for Pelé is overwhelmingly about match statistics, goals, and World Cup outcomes rather than personal behavioral or biographical detail, and per this rubric's 'success != high score' rule, competitive outcomes alone cannot support most trait scores. Unlike Muhammad Ali (extensive personal interviews, an autobiography, and a dedicated archive center), no comparably rich first-person or close-biographical source was readily available in this pass to responsibly clear the 18-attribute floor. Held, not rejected — a future pass drawing on Portuguese-language biographical sources or his own memoirs could likely responsibly clear this candidate.

provenance.notes: Second-batch diversity pick that deliberately tests the SAME thin-personal-documentation failure mode as Jesse Owens (batch 1), this time for a non-US, non-English-primary-source athlete — a genuinely distinct sourcing-access dimension worth recording, not just a repeat finding. latin_america, 20th_century, athletics.
